newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission news release on legal aspect of euro.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission news release on legal aspect of euro.

text.p: The following is a news release from the European Commission on its October 16 proposals on the legal framework for the euro.
THE LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR THE USE OF THE EURO

The European Commission today adopted proposals on the legal framework for the use of the euro. This draft legislation confirms that the euro will be the single currency of participating countries from 1 January 1999 and provides the necessary legal certainty in particular for operators in the financial markets. The main points include confirmation of the name of the euro and that it will be divided into 100 cents, continuity of contracts, 1 to 1 equivalence between the euro and the basket ECU from 1 January 1999, legal tender issues and rounding rules for conversion between national currencies and the euro. During a transitional period (1 January 1999 to 31 December 2001 at the latest) national currencies will remain in circulation, and will have equivalent legal status to the euro. Euro denominated bank notes and coins will be introduced from 1 January 2002 at the latest and will circulate in parallel with national notes and coins for up to six months, after which time only euro notes and coins will be legal tender.

The text is presented at the initiative of President SANTER, Yves- Thibault de SILGUY, Commissioner for Economic, Financial and Monetary Affairs, and Mario MONTI, Commissioner for the Single Market and Financial Services. It has been prepared following close consultation with representatives of the financial sector and their legal advisors as well as business representatives and consumer groups. It also reflects numerous contacts with member states, in particular the discussion at the informal meeting of Finance Ministers and central bank governors in Dublin on 21 September and has benefited from valuable input from the EMI.

The Madrid European Council in December 1995 recognized the need for legal certainty surrounding the introduction of the single currency. It therefore decided on the need for Community legislation to provide the legal framework for the use of the euro and set a clear timetable for its technical preparation. Additionally, numerous contacts with financial markets as well as public administrations have made it clear that the concrete preparations in the private as well as the public sector call for a timely clarification of the legal framework for the changeover to the euro.
The main objectives of the legislation are:

- to establish that from 1 January 1999 the euro shall be the currency of participating Member States, with the euro being expressed, during the transitional period (1 January 1999 until 31 December 2001, at the latest) in terms of the national currency units, thus ensuring a legally enforceable equivalence between the euro and the national currency units;

- to confirm that notes and coins denominated in euro will be introduced from 1 January 2002 at the latest and will immediately have legal tender status in all participating countries. For at most 6 months after 1 January 2002, banknotes and coins denominated in national currencies will continue to have legal tender status in their own countries. During this period, euro notes and coins will circulate alongside national notes and coins. Thereafter only euro notes and coins will be in circulation;

- to confirm the specific name "euro" instead of the generic term "ECU" used by the Treaty. The euro shall be divided into 100 cents, although this will not prevent the use of national linguistic variants of this term in common usage;
- to confirm that from 1 January 1999 the basket ECU shall be substituted for the euro at a conversion rate of one for one;

- to confirm the general principle of continuity of contracts originally denominated in ECU or a national currency. Unless specifically specified otherwise, other details of the contract (for instance expiry date or interest rates) will remain unchanged;

- to establish certain rounding rules which are important for preparations of computer systems. For example, the conversion rates between the euro and participating currencies will be set to six significant figures;
- provide for member states to ensure adequate sanctions against counterfeiting of bank notes and coins.
The intention is for the Council to come to agreement on all these elements by the Dublin European Council in mid December. Formally however, there will be two legal texts:

* a Council regulation based on Article 235 of the Treaty covering those aspects which need to come into force as soon as possible to provide the market certainty for the early preparation of the changeover. This concerns the name of the euro, continuity of contracts, the 1 for 1 equivalence between the ECU basket and the euro and the rounding rules;

* a Council regulation based on Article 109l(4) of the Treaty covering the other provisions defining the legal framework. This legal base specifically provides for the Council to adopt measures for the rapid introduction of the euro. However it only becomes operational once the list of participating countries has been decided in early 1998.

The timetable for the generalisation of the use of the euro for public sector operations as well as other preparatory measures that may be needed may be laid down in separate texts in accordance with the scenario adopted by the Madrid European Council. END OF DOCUMENT
